newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Electrolux cuts more stringent than expected.
newsitem.headline: Electrolux cuts more stringent than expected.

text.p: The world's largest appliance maker, Sweden's Electrolux AB, said Thursday it will close about 25 plants and cut 12,000 jobs in a two-year restructuring programme.

After just two months at the helm, new managing director Michael Treschow announced Electrolux would close about 25 of 150 plants and cut 12,000 staff from a workforce of 105,000 in a 2.5 billion Swedisn crown ($322 million) programme.

Analyst Andrew Griffin from UBS said the market had expected Treschow, head of industrial engineer Atlas Copco until April this year and known as a cost-cutter, to take strong measures to combat Electrolux's falling profits and tough conditions in Europe.
"But this is much stronger than people anticipated," Griffin said. "This is much more radical than anything Electrolux has done before."

Analysts say Electrolux stock has been weighed down for several years by shrinking markets and by a perception that former Chief Executive Leif Johansson -- now head of car maker Volvo -- was not tackling the roots of the company's problems.
"(Electrolux) needed to do something about its profitabilty and that was what Mr Treschow was brought in to do," said a Stockholm-based broker.
Analyst Angelica Hanson from Matteus brokerage welcomed the restructuring programme.
Electrolux said the restructuring costs levied in the second quarter would be partly offset by a capital gain of 600 million crowns ($77 million) from the sale of Husqvarna Sewing Machines.
Griffin said Treschow's plan gave the market some hope that he would also split off other parts of the group.
Electrolux said in a statement that the restructuring was designed to boost profit margins.
In 1996, Electrolux posted a 19 percent drop in profit after financial items of 3.25 billion crowns ($42 million), blaming weak European markets.
In the first quarter of 1997, Electrolux's profit dipped 14 percent against a year ago, again attributed to the difficult market situation in Europe.
